entities.name: Church of North India
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of North India (CNI), inaugurated November 29, 1970 in Nagpur, is a united Protestant church formed through the merger of six denominations (Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian, Congregationalist, Church of the Brethren, and Disciples of Christ) — the second great church union in the Indian subcontinent after the Church of South India (CSI, 1947). With 1.5 million members in 26 dioceses across North India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, CNI represents the most geographically extensive successful Protestant church union in world history, bringing together traditions from both episcopal and non-episcopal church governments.

The Church of North India was the product of decades of ecumenical negotiation — beginning in the 1920s under the influence of Bishop V.S. Azariah (India's first Anglican bishop, consecrated 1912) — that sought to overcome the denominational divisions European missionaries had imported to India. The theological challenge was significant: merging episcopal churches (Anglican, Methodist with bishops) with non-episcopal churches (Presbyterian, Congregationalist with elder-based governance) required creating a new episcopal structure acceptable to all parties.

The 1970 merger — achieved 23 years after the CSI — was celebrated as an ecumenical milestone: the integration of episcopal and non-episcopal traditions in a single church had been declared impossible by many Anglican theologians. CNI's inauguration service involved 'service of unification' that ordained all ministers from non-episcopal traditions in an episcopal laying-on-of-hands — creating a unified ordained ministry. CNI partnered with CSI in 2004 to form the National Council of Churches of India's united front, together serving over 5 million Indian Christians.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of North India — achieving the integration of episcopal and non-episcopal Protestant traditions that Anglican theologians had called impossible, across six denominations spanning three nations — is the most complex successful Protestant church union in history and the definitive model for interdenominational merger.
